opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a great question, and it gets at a real shift in the industry.

For most of the last decade, the focus was on training. You build bigger and bigger clusters, and what matters is raw throughput: how many FLOPs you can throw at the problem and how efficiently you can keep thousands of GPUs busy. GPUs are fantastic at that. They were really built for that world.

But the frontier labs have moved into a phase where inference is the dominant workload, and inference has a very different shape. Once you deploy these models to hundreds of millions of users, and especially once you move into reasoning models and agentic workflows, the bottleneck isn't compute anymore. It's memory bandwidth and latency. When a model is generating tokens one at a time, every token means streaming weights and the KV cache through memory. A GPU spends a lot of that time waiting on data rather than doing math. So you pay a lot of money and power for silicon that's underutilized.

Latency matters more now for a few reasons. First, reasoning models "think" before they answer. They might generate thousands of internal tokens. If each token is slow, the user waits a long time, or you cut the reasoning short and get a worse answer. Fast token generation directly improves quality.

Second, agents. When AI systems call tools, call other models, and run multi-step workflows, latencies compound. A small delay per step becomes a big delay across a chain of steps. Low latency is what makes those experiences feel interactive rather than like a batch job.

Third, economics. Labs want to serve more users per watt and per dollar. If you can deliver tokens faster and more efficiently, you get better unit economics on every query, and that's what makes these businesses sustainable at scale.

So the point isn't that GPUs go away. They're still the right tool for training and for a lot of high-throughput work. But the labs are realizing they need a heterogeneous infrastructure, with purpose-built inference hardware alongside the GPUs to handle the latency-sensitive, memory-bound part of the workload. That's what we've been building at d-Matrix: compute architectures that bring memory and compute much closer together, so you aren't constantly shuttling data back and forth. That's where the latency and energy savings come from.

I think we'll look back on this period as when the industry recognized that one architecture doesn't fit every job, and that inference deserves hardware designed for it from the ground up.

r001.rationale: The response says low latency can make agent workflows feel interactive and contrasts inference hardware with GPUs, but it does not state that low-latency solutions are more interactive than HBM-based GPUs or other HBM-based accelerators.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thank you for having me. Look, I think the simplest way to put it is that the hardware these labs have today was built for a different job. GPUs are phenomenal at training. You have enormous batches of data, you're doing massive matrix multiplications, and throughput is king. Latency doesn't matter much when you're running a training job for three months. But the world has shifted. The economic value of these models is now in inference, in actually serving them to users and to other software, and inference is a fundamentally different workload.

When you're generating tokens, you're doing it one at a time, sequentially, and each step depends on the one before it. That's a memory-bound problem, not a compute-bound problem. You're constantly moving model weights and the KV cache back and forth between memory and the compute units, and GPUs, for all their raw horsepower, spend a lot of their time waiting on memory. So you end up with this situation where the labs have billions of dollars of silicon that's underutilized for the thing that actually makes them money.

And the second piece is what's happening with reasoning models and agents. A year or two ago, a model would answer your question in a single forward pass. Now the model thinks. It generates thousands of tokens of internal reasoning before it gives you an answer, and then it might call a tool, read the result, and do it again. If each of those steps is slow, the whole chain becomes unusable. Agentic workflows multiply latency. So low latency isn't a nice-to-have anymore, it's the difference between a product that feels alive and one that people abandon.

So what we're seeing is the labs realizing they don't want to rip out their GPU infrastructure. They've made that investment and it's great for training and for high-throughput batch work. What they need is to augment it with something purpose-built for the latency-sensitive, memory-bound part of the workload, where you keep weights close to compute, you minimize data movement, and you get predictable, fast token generation. That's the gap, and that's why you see so much energy going into inference-specific architectures right now.

r001.rationale: The response says lower latency can make products feel more responsive and contrasts purpose-built inference systems with GPUs, but it does not state that they offer greater interactivity than HBM-based GPUs or other HBM-based accelerators.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that AI is moving from generating an answer in one pass to doing more work at inference time. A model might reason through a problem, call a tool, look at the result, and then decide what to do next. Those steps depend on one another, so latency starts to compound. If each step takes too long, the whole experience becomes impractical.

That’s why I see low-latency computing as a complement to the hardware these labs already have. You still need tremendous compute capacity for training and for serving lots of requests. But you also need to move an individual request through those sequential steps quickly. Lower latency gives you room to do more reasoning within the amount of time a user is willing to wait. It becomes a way to deliver more capable AI, as well as a faster response.

r001.rationale: The response says lower latency speeds sequential inference steps, but it does not state that these solutions offer greater interactivity than HBM-based GPUs or accelerators.

sol-6.1.text:
The reason is that AI is moving from generating an answer in one pass to doing more work at inference time. A model might reason through several steps, call a tool, look at the result, and then decide what to do next. Those steps are often sequential, so the latency of each one adds up.

The hardware frontier labs already have is very good at delivering throughput, particularly when you can batch a lot of work together. But throughput and responsiveness are different things. If you’re building an agent that takes dozens of steps to complete a task, you need each step to happen quickly enough that the whole experience is useful.

So low-latency computing complements that existing infrastructure. You still need enormous compute capacity for training and serving at scale, but you also need a fast path for workloads where the next computation depends on the previous result. That lets you spend more computation on an answer without making the user wait an unreasonable amount of time.

r001.rationale: The response says low latency improves responsiveness for sequential workloads, but it does not state that these solutions offer greater interactivity than HBM-based GPUs or other HBM-based accelerators.
